newsitem.title: FRANCE: France, Germany seek agreement on EU reform.
newsitem.headline: France, Germany seek agreement on EU reform.

text.p: The foreign ministers of France and Germany met on Wednesday to try to overcome differences on reform of the European Union ahead of a special summit of the 15-nation bloc in Dublin on Saturday.

Diplomats said Herve de Charette and Klaus Kinkel would hold a news conference but not issue any policy document because Paris and Bonn did not want to give their EU partners the impression that the Franco-German axis was dictating to others.
But they said the two ministers and their negotiators would discuss ways of giving new momentum to the Intergovernmental Conference (IGC) on EU institutional reform.
President Jacques Chirac and Chancellor Helmut Kohl would outline joint proposals to the other EU leaders in a letter in November ahead of a second summit in Dublin in December, they said.
The two main issues on which France and Germany disagree are the appointment of an EU foreign policy "tsar" and the powers of the European Parliament and of national parliaments in a reformed Union.

They agree on the need to boost the EU's fledgling common foreign and security policy by appointing a senior official to represent the bloc on the world scene and head a policy unit answerable to the Union's foreign ministers.

But while France wants a "high representative" of the level of former Swedish prime minister Carl Bildt or former Spanish prime minister Felipe Gonzalez reporting directly to heads of state and government, Germany wants a lower-level "general secretary" reporting to foreign ministers.

Bonn wants to extend the European Parliament's power of "co-decision" on EU affairs, while Paris is determined to hold the Strasbourg-based assembly to its current limited powers and ensure national parliaments are consulted in advance of decisions on justice and home affairs.

Both countries agree on the need to change the weighted voting system to give the big member states more weight relative to the smaller ones as a prelude to the enlargement of the EU to take in former communist Central European states.
But a survey this week showed that Germany's government ministries do not yet agree among themselves on which areas qualified majority voting should be extended to.
